kernelIdea: (g∘f)(s) = g(f(s)) is defined when the codomain of f is the domain of g. Composition preserves injectivity and preserves surjectivity.

kernels.l1: Two machines in a row make one bigger machine.
kernels.l2: You can run one machine and then feed its answer into another. This only works if the second machine takes what the first one gives out.
kernels.l3: Running one machine and then a second gives a new machine, and it only works when the first machine's outputs are things the second knows what to do with.
kernels.l4: Doing one function after another gives a new function, defined whenever the first one's outputs are legal inputs for the second. If both are one-to-one so is the composition, and if both are onto so is the composition.
kernels.l5: Composition is defined when codomain meets domain; it preserves injectivity and surjectivity, and the partial converses are worth knowing.
kernels.l6: Composition is associative, and composing with the do-nothing rule changes nothing on either side. It also preserves injectivity and surjectivity separately.
kernels.l7: Composition is defined when the first function's codomain is the second's domain. It preserves one-to-one and onto, and satisfies partial converses identifying which factor must be well behaved.
kernels.l8: Composition applies one function after another, is associative, and has the do-nothing rule as its unit. It is never commutative in general, and the chain rule is a theorem about it.

kernel: (g∘f)(s) = g(f(s)) is defined when f's codomain is g's domain. Composition preserves injectivity and preserves surjectivity.
objectives: Prove that the composition of injections is an injection
